notes.h: Location, size and the region studied
notes.b: The region studied is the Republic of India. Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal are referred to only as neighbours, so keep them out of your answers as parts of the region.
points: India is part of South Asia, a subcontinent (a large landmass that is part of a continent but distinct from the rest of it), bounded by the Himalayas to the north, the Arabian Sea to the west and the Bay of Bengal to the east.
India is the world's seventh-largest country by area, about 3.3 million km².
The Tropic of Cancer (the line of latitude north of the equator, marking the northern edge of the tropics) crosses central India, so much of the country lies in the tropics.
Neighbours, which are not part of the region studied: Pakistan to the west, China and Nepal to the north, Bangladesh to the east.
The republic has 28 states and 8 union territories (areas ruled more directly by the central government); its capital is New Delhi.
India is treated as a subcontinental region because of its size, the Himalayan barrier that gives it physical unity, and its own cultural and economic identity.
notes.tip: The region is the Republic of India. Don't treat Pakistan or Bangladesh as part of it.

notes.b: A sketch map earns marks for an accurate outline and for showing and naming each feature asked for. Names may go on the map itself or in a key, so choose one named example of each feature and learn where it goes.
points: Outline: a triangular peninsula (land almost surrounded by sea) tapering to the south, with a north-eastern lobe around Bangladesh.

Relief (the shape of the land), one option: outline the Himalayas as a band along the northern border, or outline the Deccan Plateau as the peninsula south of the Narmada, between the Western and Eastern Ghats.

River: the Ganges, drawn from the Himalayas in Uttarakhand south-east across the northern plain, past Varanasi, to its delta (the fan of land where a river splits and meets the sea) on the Bay of Bengal. Show it within India, ending at the delta.

Urban centres as dots on the correct river or coast: Mumbai on the west coast; Kolkata on the Hooghly near the Bay of Bengal; Delhi on the Yamuna in the north; Chennai on the east coast; Bengaluru on the southern Deccan.
Agricultural region as an outlined area: Punjab in the north-west (wheat and the Green Revolution, the introduction of high-yielding crops and modern inputs), or Assam (tea, Brahmaputra valley).
Industrial region as an outlined area: the Chota Nagpur Plateau and Damodar valley, north-east of the Deccan around Jamshedpur, or Mumbai–Pune.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the outline, a named relief feature shown as an outline, the course of a named river, one or two named urban centres and sometimes an outlined agricultural or industrial region. Prefer the Ganges as your river: the Indus flows mostly through Pakistan, and the lower Ganges and Brahmaputra and most of their delta lie in Bangladesh.

notes.h: Tropical monsoon climate and the seasons
notes.b: India's climate is dominated by the monsoon, which divides the year into three seasons. Understanding the monsoon explains most of India's farming, rivers and hazards.
points: India has a tropical monsoon climate. A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of wind direction, not simply a wet period, so the winds blow from a different direction in summer and in winter.
The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word for season.
Hot season: March to May, with the hottest conditions on the northern plains, because they are far inland and the land heats strongly before the rains.
Wet south-west monsoon: June to September, bringing most of the year's rain, because moist winds from the ocean blow onto the land.
Cool dry season: October to February, when most of India is dry because the winds blow off the land.
The monsoon retreats in October and November, marking the change between the wet and dry seasons.
notes.tip: Say that monsoon means a seasonal reversal of the winds. Don't say it rains everywhere all summer: the monsoon has breaks and is unreliable.

notes.b: The summer monsoon is driven by heating of the land and by the movement of global wind belts. Follow the steps in order, because each one causes the next.
points: 1. Intense heating of the land in early summer creates low pressure (rising warm air) over north-west India and the Tibetan Plateau, which draws in air from the cooler ocean.
2. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ, the belt near the equator where trade winds from both hemispheres meet) shifts north over India.

3. South-east trade winds (steady winds blowing towards the equator) cross the equator and are deflected by the Coriolis force (the effect of the Earth's spin, which bends winds) into south-west winds.
4. These winds pick up moisture over the Indian Ocean and reach the land as the monsoon.
5. The subtropical westerly jet stream (a fast, high-altitude river of air) moves north of the Himalayas in early summer, and the monsoon arrives suddenly, a 'burst'.
6. The jet stream returns south of the Himalayas in winter, when the monsoon withdraws.
notes.tip: If asked for the cause of the monsoon, give the heating of the land and low pressure, the northward shift of the ITCZ, the deflected trade winds and the jet stream moving north of the Himalayas.

notes.h: Onset, timing and the two branches
notes.b: The monsoon does not arrive everywhere at once. It sweeps north in two branches, which hit different parts of India first.
points: The south-west monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by mid-July.
It brings about three-quarters of India's annual rainfall, falling mainly in June to September, so the other eight months share the remaining quarter.
The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats (the mountain range along the west coast) first, dropping heavy rain on the windward side, the side facing the wind.
The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the north-east hills, then is turned west along the Ganges plain by the Himalayas, bringing rain eastwards and along the plain.
notes.tip: Name both branches and say where each strikes first: the Arabian Sea branch hits the Western Ghats, the Bay of Bengal branch hits the north-east hills and is then turned west along the Ganges plain.

notes.h: Relief rainfall, rain shadow and the rainfall gradient
notes.b: Rainfall in India depends on where the monsoon winds meet high ground. Mountains force moist air up, making one side very wet and the other dry.
points: Relief (orographic) rain: moist air is forced up the windward slopes of the Western Ghats, cools and drops its rain, giving heavy rain on the Konkan and Malabar coasts.
The Deccan Plateau behind the Western Ghats lies in their rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of mountains, where the air has already lost its moisture) and is much drier.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, are among the wettest places on earth, due to relief rain from the Bay of Bengal branch.
Rainfall falls off westwards along the Ganges plain: Kolkata in the east is wetter than Delhi in the north-west, because the winds lose moisture as they travel inland.
The Thar Desert in Rajasthan is the driest region, because the Arabian Sea branch passes parallel to the Aravalli Range and has no barrier to force it upwards.
notes.tip: Examiners expect relief rain and rain shadow explained with the Western Ghats and the Deccan. For the Thar Desert, say there is no barrier to force the air up. Don't give rainfall totals.

notes.h: The cool dry season and winter rain
notes.b: In winter the wind pattern reverses and India is mostly dry, but there are two regional exceptions. Both matter for farming.
points: High pressure over Central Asia gives north-east winds that blow off the land, so most of India is dry in winter, because air from land carries little moisture.
The Himalayas shelter India from cold air from Central Asia.
Exception: the Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast receives most of its rain from the north-east monsoon, as these winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.
Western disturbances (depressions from the west, areas of low pressure that move in) bring light winter rain to the north-west, which is important for wheat.
notes.tip: The north-east (winter) monsoon is dry for most of India but wet on the Tamil Nadu coast. Mention this exception.

notes.b: India lies mostly in the tropics, so heat is the norm. Only height above sea level and the season change it much.
points: The hot season brings high temperatures to the northern plains, often above 40°C, with hot, dry winds called loo.
The south stays hot all year.
The Himalayas are cold, so temperatures fall with altitude (height above sea level).

notes.b: The monsoon is not reliable, and both too little and too much rain cause disasters. Climate change is adding to the risk.
points: A late, weak or broken monsoon (one with long dry breaks) causes drought, because crops and reservoirs depend on its rain.
A heavy monsoon causes floods, because rivers receive more water than their channels can carry.
Tropical cyclones (violent rotating storms that form over warm seas) strike the east coast, mainly in the pre-monsoon and retreating-monsoon periods.
Odisha super cyclone, October 1999: about 10,000 deaths, an example of how deadly a storm on the east coast can be.
Climate change is making the monsoon more erratic (so drought and flood risks both rise) and heatwaves more severe.
notes.tip: Use drought for a late, weak or broken monsoon and floods for a heavy one, and give the Odisha cyclone of 1999 as your example.

notes.b: Because most Indians depend on farming, the timing and strength of the monsoon shape the whole economy.
points: Its timing decides the farming calendar, so a late monsoon delays sowing, with kharif crops (sown with the monsoon) and rabi crops (sown after it), which are covered under the farming calendar below.
It refills reservoirs and groundwater, which supply irrigation and drinking water.
Because farming is a large part of the economy, a poor monsoon affects GDP (the total value of what the country produces).

notes.b: Soil type follows the parent material (the rock or sediment the soil forms from) and the climate. Alluvial soil is India's most extensive soil type.
points: Alluvial soils (soils made of silt and sand laid down by rivers) are the most extensive and most fertile, found on the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the eastern deltas.
They are deposited by Himalayan rivers, which carry silt down from the mountains, forming newer khadar (floodplain) soils and older bhangar (higher terraces).
Desert soils in the Thar, Rajasthan, are sandy, so they hold little water, low in humus (decayed plant matter that feeds soil) and sometimes saline (salty).
Desert soils are productive only where canal irrigation reaches them: the Indira Gandhi Canal, Rajasthan, brings water from Punjab's rivers into the Thar Desert.

notes.b: Black soils form on volcanic rock and are among the best soils of the Deccan for one particular crop.
points: Black soils (regur, or black cotton soil) are weathered (broken down) from the basalt lava (dark volcanic rock) of the Deccan Traps in north-west Deccan, Maharashtra.
They are clay-rich, so they hold moisture well.
They crack deeply when dry, a feature sometimes called self-ploughing, because the cracks let air and water into the soil.
They are ideal for cotton, the main crop on the Deccan Traps, because cotton needs soil that keeps moisture.
notes.tip: Black soil comes from basalt, the Deccan Traps.

notes.b: Red soils form on old, hard rock and are poorer than black soils.
points: Red soils are weathered from ancient crystalline rocks (hard rocks made of interlocking crystals, here granite and gneiss) of the south and east Deccan.
They are red because of iron oxide (rust), and are low in nitrogen and humus.
They support millets (small-seeded drought-tolerant cereals), groundnuts and pulses (beans, peas and lentils), and give better yields with fertiliser and irrigation.
notes.tip: Red soil comes from older granite and gneiss, not from basalt.

notes.b: Laterite forms where heat and heavy rain wash goodness out of the ground. It is a poor soil for farming, though it has a use in building.
points: Laterite forms under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, which leach out (wash away) silica and nutrients, leaving iron and aluminium oxides behind.
Laterite is found on the Western Ghats and in Kerala.
It is infertile because the leaching removed the nutrients, but with fertiliser it supports tea, coffee and cashew.
It hardens when exposed to air, so it is cut into building bricks.
notes.tip: Laterite comes from intense leaching. Don't call it fertile.

notes.b: On steep Himalayan slopes soil cannot build up, so farming depends on cutting flat steps into the hillside.
points: Mountain soils on the Himalayan slopes are thin and immature (not yet developed into deep, layered soil).
On the terraces (flat steps cut into the slopes, which give level ground on steep land) tea and fruit are grown.

notes.b: Farming and the monsoon together damage India's soils in three main ways.
points: Erosion (the wearing away of soil): monsoon downpours and deforestation create gullies and ravines, such as the Chambal ravines of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
Salinisation (salt build-up in the soil) and waterlogging (soil saturated with water) occur under canal irrigation in Punjab and Haryana.
Nutrient exhaustion results from intensive Green Revolution farming, which takes crop after crop from the same land.

notes.b: Two Indian soils show how rock type and weathering link to soil.
points: Basalt weathers to black soil, so black soils are tied to soils to the Deccan Traps, the thick basalt layers covered under the relief notes below.
Laterite is the product of intense chemical weathering (rock broken down by chemical reactions) in hot, wet conditions.

notes.b: Relief means the shape and height of the land. India has three main relief divisions, with the Thar Desert, the coastal plains and the islands added to them.
points: The Himalayas lie to the north, forming India's mountain wall.
The Northern Plains, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, lie in front of the Himalayas, where the rivers spread their silt.
The Peninsular Plateau, the Deccan, forms the southern peninsula.
Coastal plains and islands lie along the coasts.

notes.b: The Himalayas form India's northern wall. They are the youngest and highest of its landforms.
points: The Himalayas are young fold mountains (formed when rock layers are crumpled up by collision) formed by the collision of the Indian (Indo-Australian) plate with the Eurasian plate. The collision began about 50 million years ago and continues.
Three parallel ranges run west to east: the Greater Himalaya (Himadri), the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks.
Kangchenjunga, 8,586 m, on the India (Sikkim)–Nepal border, is India's highest peak and the world's third highest.
Mount Everest (8,849 m) is on the Nepal–China border, not in India.
notes.tip: Everest is not in India. India's highest peak is Kangchenjunga. Don't put volcanoes in the Himalayas, which formed at a collision boundary.

notes.b: The Himalayas shape India's climate, rivers and settlement. Their effects are both helpful and harmful.
points: The mountains are a barrier to cold air from Central Asia.
They trigger monsoon rain, as the monsoon is forced upwards by the mountain wall.
Perennial rivers (rivers that flow all year) fed by snow melt rise in the Himalayas.
The rivers have hydroelectric potential (power from falling water) because they drop steeply.
The mountains are a barrier to transport and are prone to earthquakes and landslides.
Settlement is sparse because of the steep, cold terrain, which makes farming and building hard.

notes.b: South of the Himalayas lies the flattest and most useful land in India.
points: The Northern Plains are vast, flat and low.
They are built from alluvium (silt and sand laid down by rivers) deposited by the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems in a trough (a long hollow) in front of the Himalayas.
They are the agricultural and population heartland of India.

notes.h: The Deccan Plateau and Deccan Traps
notes.b: The Deccan is an old, stable upland that covers most of southern India. Part of it is covered by lava from ancient eruptions.
points: The Deccan Plateau is very old, made of hard crystalline rock, so it forms a stable shield (a block of ancient rock that is no longer folded or moved much).
It was once part of the ancient Gondwanaland landmass, the supercontinent that later broke apart.
The plateau tilts from west to east, so most of its rivers flow east.
The Chota Nagpur Plateau in the north-east of the plateau is rich in minerals, such as coal and iron ore.

The Deccan Traps are thick layers of basalt from huge fissure eruptions (lava pouring from long cracks) about 66 million years ago, covering much of the north-west Deccan (the source of the black soils).

notes.b: Two mountain ranges edge the Deccan Plateau, one on each coast. They differ in height and continuity.
points: The Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri, form a steep, continuous escarpment (a long steep slope) along the west coast.
The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) for their biodiversity (the variety of living things).
Anamudi, 2,695 m, in Kerala, is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas.
The Eastern Ghats are lower and broken into separate hills, because east-flowing rivers cut through them.

notes.h: Other ranges and the Thar Desert
notes.b: Between the plains and the plateau, and in the north-west, are older ranges that also shape drainage and rainfall.
points: The Vindhya and Satpura ranges separate the plains from the Deccan, forming a divide between north and south.
The Narmada flows west between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
The Aravalli Range, Rajasthan, is among the oldest fold mountains on earth.
The Thar Desert lies west of the Aravalli Range, on the dry side where the monsoon winds are not forced upwards.

notes.b: Narrow plains run along both coasts, but the west and east differ in width and in what the rivers have built.
points: The narrow western plain includes the Konkan coast (Maharashtra, Goa) in the north and the Malabar coast (Kerala) in the south, with backwaters and lagoons (shallow coastal waters partly cut off from the sea).
The wider eastern plain is the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu), with large river deltas, because the Deccan's rivers flow east and deposit silt there.

notes.b: Each relief division supports a different way of life, which is why people and industry are spread unevenly.
points: The plains support dense population, intensive farming and easy transport, because the land is flat and fertile.
The plateau is rich in minerals, so it supports industry.
The mountains support tourism and hydroelectricity, with sparse settlement because the land is steep and cold.

notes.b: India's rivers fall into two groups. The Himalayan and peninsular rivers differ in their source, flow and seasonal regime (how their flow changes through the year).
points: Himalayan rivers are perennial, because they are fed by snow and glacier melt plus monsoon rain, and are large, with high flows in summer.
Peninsular rivers are seasonal, because they are rain-fed, so they are low in the dry season, and shorter.
Peninsular rivers flow in older, harder rock, with fixed valleys, so they cannot easily shift course.

notes.b: The Ganges is India's most important river. It drains the largest basin in the country and feeds the Northern Plains.
points: The Ganges rises as the Bhagirathi at Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand.
It becomes the Ganga where the Bhagirathi meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag.
It flows past Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj (Allahabad), Varanasi and Patna.
The Yamuna, a tributary (a river that joins a larger one) which flows past Delhi and Agra, joins it at Prayagraj.
The river is about 2,500 km long and its basin (the area drained by it and its tributaries) covers about a quarter of India, the largest basin in India.
It enters Bangladesh and joins the Brahmaputra to form the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, the world's largest delta; the delta is shared with Bangladesh.
The Sundarbans mangrove forest (trees that grow in salty coastal mud), home of the Bengal tiger, lies on the delta across India and Bangladesh.
The Hooghly, a distributary (a branch that leaves the main river), flows through Kolkata, which is why the city is a river port.
notes.tip: For a sketch map, show the Ganges within India, ending at the delta. Don't call the Sundarbans wholly Indian: they span India and Bangladesh.

notes.b: The Brahmaputra drains the north-east and carries so much sediment that it floods the same area every year.
points: The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo.
It enters India in Arunachal Pradesh and flows west through Assam.
It joins the Ganges in Bangladesh.
It is braided (split into many shifting channels around sandbanks) and carries huge loads of silt, so its channels clog and it floods Assam annually.

notes.b: The Indus is a Himalayan river that mostly flows outside India, yet its tributaries water India's wheat belt.
points: The Indus rises in Tibet and flows through Ladakh into Pakistan, mostly through Pakistan.
Its five Punjab tributaries are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
Its waters irrigate India's wheat belt in the Punjab, which is why the Indus matters to India even though it flows mostly through Pakistan.
The Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, 1960, brokered by the World Bank, divides its waters.

notes.b: Because the Deccan Plateau tilts eastwards, its main rivers cross it to reach the Bay of Bengal.
points: The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow east to the Bay of Bengal.
The Godavari is the longest river of peninsular India, which is the name for the southern triangle of the country.
They build deltas on the Bay of Bengal coast, which are fertile rice lands because of the silt they deposit.
The Kaveri (Cauvery) water dispute is between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, two states that both want the river's water.

notes.b: Two peninsular rivers run against the general eastward tilt and reach the Arabian Sea.
points: The Narmada and the Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.
They flow through rift valleys (long valleys formed where land has dropped between faults) and end in estuaries (wide river mouths affected by the tide), not deltas.

notes.b: Rivers on the flat plains both create and destroy. Their floods bring fertile silt but also loss.
points: Monsoon floods occur on the Ganges plain and in Bihar and Assam, because the rivers swell with monsoon rain and snow melt.
Silt deposition renews soils, but floods destroy crops and homes.
The Kosi, a Ganges tributary in Bihar, is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' because of its floods and shifting course; it broke its embankment in 2008.
Rivers shift course on the flat plains, because there is little slope to hold them in one channel.

notes.b: People try to control the rivers so that water is available all year and floods are reduced. This brings benefits and conflict.
points: Multipurpose dams (dams built for several uses at once) provide irrigation, hydroelectricity and flood control.
Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej, Himachal Pradesh, supplies irrigation water and power to Punjab and Haryana.
Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada, Gujarat, brings irrigation and drinking water to Gujarat but displaced many thousands of villagers.
The displacement led to the Narmada Bachao Andolan ('Save the Narmada') protest movement.
Canal irrigation spreads water beyond the river valleys, so dry land far from a river can be farmed.
Water is disputed between states, as in the Kaveri dispute, and with neighbouring countries, as in the Indus Waters Treaty.

notes.b: The same river that millions depend on is heavily polluted, and governments have launched clean-up programmes.
points: The Ganges is polluted by sewage, industrial waste and cremations.
Ritual bathing and cremation take place along the river at Varanasi, which adds to the pollution because ashes and waste enter the water.
The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985.
The Namami Gange programme followed in 2014.

notes.b: Rivers are central to religion and daily life as well as to the economy.
points: The Ganges is sacred to Hindus, so millions bathe in it and visit it.
Rivers provide water for drinking, irrigation and transport, such as boats on the Ganges.
The rivers' floods deposit fertile alluvium on the plains, sustaining farming and settlement.

notes.b: Agriculture is the biggest employer in India but contributes far less to the economy than its workforce suggests.
points: Agriculture employs the largest share of workers: in Census 2011, about 55% of workers were cultivators or agricultural labourers.
It produces a much smaller share of GDP, under a fifth in the early 2020s, which shows low productivity (little output per worker).
Its share of employment is falling, as more people move into industry and services.
notes.tip: Contrast the large share of workers with the small share of GDP, which shows low productivity.

notes.b: Indian farming ranges from tiny family plots to large commercial farms. Each type suits a particular region and climate.
points: Subsistence farming (growing food mainly for the farmer's own family) on small plots, so little is left to sell.
Intensive wet-rice (paddy) farming in the wet east, the south and the deltas, where rain and flooded fields suit rice.
Commercial irrigated wheat farming (growing for sale, using canal or well water) in the north-west, in Punjab and Haryana.
Plantation farming (large estates growing one crop for sale): tea in Assam and Darjeeling (West Bengal), and in the Nilgiri Hills (Tamil Nadu); coffee in Karnataka.
Cash crops (crops grown to sell): cotton on black soils in Maharashtra and Gujarat, sugar cane, and jute in West Bengal.
Dairy farming, such as the co-operatives described under the White Revolution, and pastoralism (herding animals) in dry areas.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to name two types of agriculture, so learn at least two with a place each.

notes.b: The monsoon splits the farming year into two main cropping seasons, kharif and rabi.
points: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon in June and July, so they use its rain, and harvested in autumn: rice, cotton, maize and millets.
Rabi crops are sown in October and November and harvested in March and April: wheat, mustard and gram.
Rabi crops depend on irrigation and on the rain from western disturbances, because the main monsoon has ended.
Kharif means monsoon (summer) crops such as rice; rabi means winter crops such as wheat.
notes.tip: Don't swap kharif and rabi: kharif is monsoon (summer) crops such as rice, rabi is winter crops such as wheat.

notes.b: India's climate, soils and rivers give farmers several natural advantages.
points: Tropical temperatures allow two or three crops a year, because there is no cold season long enough to stop growth.
The monsoon provides seasonal rain.
Fertile alluvium covers the plains, and black soil covers the Deccan, so both regions grow crops well.
The land is flat across the plains, easing cultivation and transport.
Perennial Himalayan rivers supply water for irrigation, so crops can be watered in the dry season.
notes.tip: Questions on factors influencing agriculture ask about climate and the monsoon, relief and soils and irrigation, so link each advantage to one of these.

notes.b: The same physical setting also limits farming in many places.
points: The monsoon is unreliable, so farmers face drought in some years and floods in others.
Laterite and desert soils are poor, because they are infertile or short of water.
Steep slopes limit cultivation, because soil is thin and machines cannot work them.
Soil erosion and salinisation reduce yields, since the soil loses its fertility.
Water tables (the level below which the ground is saturated) are falling, as more water is pumped out than the rain refills.

notes.b: Irrigation (supplying water to crops by artificial means) makes farming possible in dry areas and in the dry season.
points: Canals in Punjab and the Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan, which brings river water into the Thar Desert, supply water.
Tubewells (deep pumped wells) draw groundwater for irrigation, which makes farming possible where there is no canal.
Irrigation was essential to the Green Revolution, because the new crop varieties needed reliable water.
Groundwater is overused in Punjab, lowering the water table.

notes.b: From the mid-1960s, a package of new methods raised food-grain output. It made India self-sufficient but brought costs.
points: High-yielding wheat varieties were developed in Mexico by Norman Borlaug; Indian scientist M. S. Swaminathan led their introduction in India.
The package included high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation and machinery.
Food-grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million tonnes (2022–23).
India became self-sufficient in food, meaning it could feed itself without relying on imports.
The core areas were Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where irrigation was already available.
Benefits were concentrated in these areas and among larger farmers, because they could afford seed, fertiliser and machinery.
Costs: groundwater depletion, soil degradation, chemical pollution and farmer debt.
notes.tip: Give both sides: the rise in output and self-sufficiency, and the costs of groundwater depletion, soil degradation, chemical pollution and debt.

notes.b: A similar push in dairying made India the world's largest producer of milk, using co-operatives (businesses owned and run by their farmer members).
points: Operation Flood, launched in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board under Verghese Kurien, built co-operative dairying.
The Amul co-operative, based at Anand, Gujarat, is a model of the system.
Operation Flood made India the world's largest milk producer, because co-operatives gave small farmers a market for their milk.
Religion supports dairying: the cow is sacred to Hindus, so cattle are kept for milk and draught (pulling ploughs and carts), not beef.

notes.h: Human and economic problems in farming
notes.b: Beyond the weather, many of farming's problems come from how land is owned and how farmers are paid.
points: Holdings are very small and fragmented: in the Agriculture Census 2015–16, the average holding was about 1.1 hectares, and about 86% of holdings were small or marginal (under 2 hectares).
Holdings are subdivided at each inheritance, because land is divided among heirs.
Landless labourers have little land of their own, so they depend on wages and are very poor.
Farmers lack capital and credit, so debt is common.
Middlemen (traders between farmer and buyer) take a share of the profit, so farmers receive less.
Poor storage and roads cause post-harvest losses, because crops spoil or cannot reach markets.
notes.tip: Holding size, capital, markets and government policy are all factors examiners ask about, so use the figures for holding size.

notes.b: Government policy and a large home market give Indian farmers some security.
points: India has a huge domestic market of over 1.4 billion people, so there is strong demand for food.
The government sets minimum support prices (guaranteed prices) and buys grain, which is stored by the Food Corporation of India.
PM-KISAN, launched in 2019, gives income support: it pays ₹6,000 a year directly to landholding farm families.
India is the world's largest rice exporter (early 2020s).

notes.b: Farming also causes distress, pollution and political conflict.
points: Drought and farmer distress, including farmer suicides, are persistent problems, because debt and crop failure leave farmers with no safety net.
Stubble burning (burning the straw left after harvest) in Punjab and Haryana, October to November, after the rice harvest, worsens Delhi's winter smog.
The 2020–21 farmers' protests, mainly by Punjab and Haryana farmers camped on Delhi's borders, opposed three farm laws.
The farm laws were repealed (withdrawn) in November 2021, after the protests.

notes.b: These rankings back up answers on the importance of Indian agriculture.
points: India is the world's second-largest producer of rice and of wheat, after China.
India is the second-largest producer of tea, after China.
India is the largest producer of jute.
India is the largest producer of milk, thanks to the White Revolution, so dairying is a major strength.
Bt (genetically modified) cotton, a variety changed to resist pests, was approved in 2002.

notes.b: Forests cover only part of India and are under pressure from people, so protection is needed.
points: Forests cover about one-fifth of India's area (early 2020s).
Tropical monsoon (deciduous, leaf-shedding) forests cover much of the country.
Wet evergreen forest grows on the Western Ghats and in the north-east.
Mangroves grow in the Sundarbans, West Bengal, a UNESCO site.
Fuelwood use (burning wood for cooking and heating) and deforestation reduce forest cover, because trees are cut faster than they regrow.
Afforestation (planting new forest) and protected areas respond to these losses; Project Tiger began in 1973.

notes.b: India's long coast and large rivers support both sea and inland fishing.
points: India has a long coastline and large rivers, which give it both sea and freshwater fishing.
Marine fishing is important in Kerala, Gujarat and West Bengal.
Inland aquaculture (fish and prawn ponds) is growing fast, because it does not depend on the sea.
India is one of the world's largest fish producers.

notes.b: India's minerals are concentrated in one upland region, which became the base of its steel industry.
points: The Chota Nagpur Plateau covers Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
It holds most of India's coal and iron ore, so it is the basis of the steel industry.
Coal is mined in the Jharia coalfield and the Damodar valley coalfields in Jharkhand.
Iron ore is also mined in Karnataka and Goa, and in Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.

notes.b: India relies on coal for most of its electricity, which brings economic gain and environmental cost.
points: India is the world's second-largest coal producer, after China.
Coal generates about 70% of India's electricity (early 2020s), which makes it the main source of power.
Coal's environmental costs include air pollution and the displacement of tribal people, who lose land where mines are opened.

notes.b: India has some oil but not enough for its needs.
points: The Mumbai High offshore oil field (drilled from the sea bed), in the Arabian Sea, was discovered in 1974.
India imports most of its crude oil, because its own output is small compared with demand.

notes.b: India is expanding sources of power that do not burn coal.
points: Hydroelectricity (power from flowing water) comes from the Himalayan rivers, which fall steeply, and from large dams.
Solar energy is expanding fastest in Rajasthan, a sunny dry state, where the Bhadla Solar Park is one of the world's largest.
Wind energy is developing in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, so power can come from sources other than coal.
India's target, announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, is 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030.

notes.b: This is background only. It explains where Indian industry first grew.
points: Britain used India as a source of raw materials and as a market for its manufactures, so Indian industry grew to serve Britain's needs.
Early industry was cotton textiles in Bombay (Mumbai) and Ahmedabad, called the 'Manchester of India', from the 19th century.
Jute mills were built along the Hooghly near Calcutta (Kolkata), close to the jute-growing delta and a port.
The Tata Iron and Steel Company, founded in 1907 at Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, was India's first large steel works, sited on Chota Nagpur coal and iron ore.

notes.b: After independence the government planned and owned much of industry, and also controlled it tightly.
points: The First Five-Year Plan began in 1951; Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister, from 1947 to 1964.
Industrialisation was state-led: the state built steel plants at Bhilai (with Soviet Union help), Rourkela (West Germany) and Durgapur (Britain).
Imports were protected from foreign competition, so Indian firms were sheltered from rivals.
The Licence Raj required permits to start or expand a factory, which made industry inefficient.
notes.tip: Two factors for manufacturing can include government policy, so know the Licence Raj and its effect.

notes.b: In 1991 India changed course and opened its economy, which sped up growth.
points: A balance-of-payments crisis (when a country cannot pay for its imports) led to reform in 1991, under Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.
Most licences were removed, tariffs (taxes on imports) were cut and India opened to foreign investment, so firms could grow and compete.
Manufacturing and services grew rapidly after 1991, because firms were freer to expand.
Export markets grew after 1991, because trade barriers were lowered.

notes.b: More recent policies try to attract firms and boost factory output.
points: Make in India was launched in 2014 to attract firms to make goods in India.
The Special Economic Zones Act was passed in 2005; Special Economic Zones offer incentives to firms, so firms are drawn to them.
Production-Linked Incentive schemes, from 2020, pay subsidies per unit produced for electronics, cars and pharmaceuticals.
Industrial corridors (planned belts of industry and transport), such as the Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor, link manufacturing sites.

notes.h: Raw materials as a location factor
notes.b: A location factor is a reason a factory is sited in one place. Raw materials were decisive for India's oldest industries.
points: Coal, iron ore, limestone and manganese of the Chota Nagpur Plateau support iron and steel, at Jamshedpur and in the state plants.
Cotton grown on black soils supports textiles in Mumbai and Ahmedabad, because mills sit near their raw material.
Jute grown in the Ganges delta supports jute mills in Kolkata, which is close by.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for two factors that influenced manufacturing, such as raw materials, markets, infrastructure, government policy, labour and transport. Give a named example with each.

notes.b: India's people are one of its main advantages for industry.
points: India has a huge, young, low-cost labour force, so wage bills are low.
It has a large pool of engineers and graduates from the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs); the first opened at Kharagpur in 1951.
Most workers are in the informal sector (jobs with no contract, regular wage or legal protection).

notes.b: Firms locate where there are customers, and India has many.
points: The domestic market of over 1.4 billion people is growing, with a rising middle class that buys cars, phones and consumer goods.
Export markets have been open to Indian manufacturers since 1991, so firms can sell abroad.

notes.b: Infrastructure means the transport and power systems that firms rely on. It is good in some places and weak in others.
points: Ports at Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata handle trade, so goods can be exported and raw materials imported.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Navi Mumbai, is one of India's main container ports.
Railways and the Golden Quadrilateral road network link factories to markets, so goods reach customers.
Infrastructure is weak in many areas, with power cuts and congestion raising costs.

notes.h: Government policy as a location factor
notes.b: Policy, not just geography, decides where industry grows.
points: Policy changed location as well as scale: licensing shaped where firms could expand, and incentive schemes now steer firms to chosen sites.
Special Economic Zones and production-linked incentives are offered by policy, not by natural resources.

notes.b: Manufacturing is concentrated in the west and south, in a few named industrial regions.
points: Mumbai–Pune, on the west coast.
Ahmedabad–Vadodara, in Gujarat.
The Hooghly belt around Kolkata, in the east.
The Chota Nagpur and Damodar valley region, around Jamshedpur.
The Delhi National Capital Region, including Gurugram and Noida.
The southern cluster of Bengaluru, Chennai and Coimbatore.
The north and east (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha) are less industrialised, in contrast with the west and south.

notes.b: Each major industry has named firms and centres you can use as examples.
points: Iron and steel: India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer (since 2018).
Cotton textiles and garments: Tiruppur, Tamil Nadu, is known for knitwear exports.
Cars: Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Suzuki of Japan, began in 1983 with the Maruti 800; its plants are at Gurugram and Manesar, Haryana. Chennai has a car cluster that includes Hyundai.

Pharmaceuticals: India is a leading maker of generic medicines (cheaper copies of branded drugs), called the 'pharmacy of the world'; Hyderabad is a major centre. The Serum Institute of India in Pune is the world's largest vaccine maker by number of doses and made the Covishield (AstraZeneca) COVID-19 vaccine.
Electronics assembly: Foxconn assembles Apple iPhones at Sriperumbudur, near Chennai.
Aerospace and defence: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and the headquarters of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) are in Bengaluru.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to name a secondary activity, its advantages and one challenge, so pick one industry and give a named example.

notes.b: Indian manufacturing faces obstacles that have held its share of the economy down.
points: Poor infrastructure and power supply raise costs.
Land acquisition causes conflict: in Singur, West Bengal, in 2008, protests over farmland taken for Tata's Nano car factory forced Tata to move the plant to Sanand, Gujarat.
Bureaucracy and complex regulation slow investment, because approvals take time.
Competition from China is strong, because Chinese manufacturing is larger.
Pollution and industrial accidents: the Bhopal gas leak of December 1984, from the Union Carbide pesticide plant, killed thousands.
Old industries have declined: the Great Bombay textile strike of 1982 led to the closure of most of Mumbai's cotton mills, whose land was later redeveloped.
Manufacturing's share of the economy has stayed low compared with China.
notes.tip: For Bhopal say 'thousands'. Don't give an exact death toll, because sources disagree widely.

notes.b: Tertiary activities (services such as IT, tourism and transport) now dominate the Indian economy.
points: Services are now the largest sector, so they matter more than farming or industry, producing over half of India's GDP (early 2020s).
India is among the world's five largest economies by GDP (early 2020s).

notes.b: Outsourcing means a foreign firm pays an Indian company to do work such as software or call-centre tasks. India's IT industry is centred on Bengaluru.
points: Bengaluru, called the 'Silicon Valley of India' after the US technology centre, is the leading IT centre.
Other IT centres are Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Gurugram and Noida.
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), founded in 1968 and based in Mumbai, is an Indian IT firm.
Infosys, founded in 1981 in Pune, has its headquarters in Bengaluru.
Wipro is based in Bengaluru.
Texas Instruments, a US firm, opened a design centre in Bengaluru in 1985, one of the first multinationals (firms operating in many countries) to do so.
notes.tip: Bollywood is in Mumbai, not Bengaluru, so don't mix up the two cities' industries.

notes.b: India's IT boom has several causes that came together, which is why exam answers need more than one.
points: A large English-speaking graduate workforce, because English is the language of business for foreign clients.
The Indian Institutes of Technology produce skilled engineers.
Low wages.
A time difference with the USA allows work round the clock.
The 1991 liberalisation opened the economy, and software technology parks were established.
Bengaluru had an early lead in public-sector science and engineering.

notes.b: India's attractions are spread across the country. Learn several, with the place each is in.
points: The Taj Mahal, Agra, on the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh, is a marble tomb built in the 17th century by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal; a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983).
The Golden Triangle links Delhi, Agra and Jaipur, the 'Pink City' of Rajasthan.
Rajasthan's forts and palaces, which show its royal history.
Goa's beaches; Goa was a Portuguese colony until 1961, so it has a distinct heritage.
Kerala's backwaters and houseboats around Alappuzha, and Ayurveda (traditional Indian medicine).
Varanasi, a Hindu holy city with bathing ghats (stone steps down to the river) on the Ganges.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for two named tourist attractions, so name the attraction and its place.

notes.h: Tourist attractions: hills, wildlife and pilgrimage
notes.b: Mountains, wildlife reserves and religious sites draw different kinds of visitor.
points: Hill stations (towns in the hills, used as cool retreats from the heat of the plains), such as Shimla, summer capital of British India, and Darjeeling.
Wildlife: Jim Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, India's first national park (1936); Ranthambore, Rajasthan, for tigers; Kaziranga, Assam, for the one-horned rhinoceros, a UNESCO site.
The Golden Temple, Amritsar, the holiest Sikh shrine.
The Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj, a vast Hindu pilgrimage gathering.

notes.b: Visitors come for a mix of culture, scenery, climate and price.
points: Culture and history: Mughal and Hindu monuments, religion and festivals.
Varied physical landscapes, from beaches and backwaters to the Himalayas.
A warm, dry winter, from October to March, matches the European winter, so it suits visitors escaping the cold.
Low costs for travellers.
Spiritual tourism, yoga, Ayurveda and medical tourism.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask why tourists come, so give reasons such as culture, landscape, climate and low costs.

notes.b: Marketing, easier visas and better air links have made it easier for visitors to reach India.
points: The 'Incredible India' marketing campaign began in 2002.
E-visas (visas applied for online) were introduced in 2014.
About 11 million foreign tourist arrivals were recorded in 2019, before COVID-19.
Airport expansion and low-cost airlines, led by IndiGo, India's largest airline, have improved access.
Domestic tourism is far larger than foreign tourism.

notes.b: Tourism brings economic and conservation benefits.
points: Jobs in hotels, guiding, crafts and transport.
Foreign currency earnings.
Investment in infrastructure.
Preservation of heritage sites and wildlife.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level asks for positive and negative impacts of tourism, so give at least one of each.

notes.h: Negative impacts and challenges of tourism
notes.b: The same visitors also damage the places they come to see.
points: Overcrowding and pollution at major sites.
Air pollution has discoloured the Taj Mahal's white marble; the Supreme Court has restricted polluting industry around it.
Water shortages and waste in Goa.
Erosion of local culture.
Seasonality: tourism peaks in the dry winter (so hotels are quiet at other times), so work is uneven through the year.
Safety and sanitation concerns, and poor infrastructure.

notes.b: Railways are the backbone of long-distance travel and freight in India, and were begun under British rule.
points: The first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853, under British rule.
Indian Railways is one of the world's largest networks, about 68,000 km long, one of the four largest in the world, and employs over 1 million people.
Rail carries huge numbers of passengers and freight, including bulky goods such as coal and grain.
The Konkan Railway, opened in 1998, runs along the west coast.
Modernisation includes dedicated freight corridors, the Vande Bharat Express (from 2019), and the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed line, under construction with Japanese funding and technology.

notes.b: Roads link towns and villages, but traffic and safety are serious problems.
points: The Golden Quadrilateral, a major road network, is about 5,800 km of upgraded highway linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, built from 2001.
The rural roads programme (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, 2000) connects villages to the network, so farmers can reach markets.
Congestion and very high road-death rates are serious problems, because roads are crowded.

notes.b: Air travel, ports and city metros complete India's transport network.
points: Domestic aviation is growing fast, because low-cost airlines have made flying cheaper.
Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi, is India's busiest airport.
Major container ports handle trade, such as Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Navi Mumbai.
Metro systems (urban railways that cut road congestion) include the Delhi Metro, opened in 2002.

notes.b: Transport ties the whole economy together.
points: Transport links farms to markets, raw materials to factories and workers to cities.
It integrates a huge country and enables tourism.
Two named types of transport: rail (Indian Railways) and road (the Golden Quadrilateral).
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for two types of transport and their importance, so give a named example of each.

notes.b: India has one of the largest populations in the world, which is measured by a census (an official count held about every ten years).
points: Census 1951 recorded about 361 million people, so the population has more than tripled by Census 2011 recorded about 1.21 billion.
Population grew about 17.7% between 2001 and 2011, so growth was still strong.
India overtook China as the world's most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate, over 1.4 billion).
The census due in 2021 was postponed, so Census 2011 remains the latest census.
notes.tip: Use Census 2011 or the labelled survey and UN figures only. Never give a 2021 census figure, because there was none.

notes.b: The demographic transition model describes how birth and death rates change as a country develops. India shows it clearly.
points: Death rates fell first, because of medicine, vaccination and better food supply from the Green Revolution, while birth rates stayed high, giving rapid growth.
The National Family Health Survey 5 (2019–21) gives a total fertility rate (average number of children per woman) of 2.0 for India, just below the replacement level of 2.1.
India is in late stage 3 (birth rates falling, so growth is slowing) of the demographic transition model, where birth rates fall and growth slows.
notes.tip: Don't use the old figure of 2.1 children per woman as India's current fertility. Use 2.0 from NFHS-5.

notes.b: National figures hide large differences between states.
points: Kerala has a total fertility rate of about 1.8 (NFHS-5, 2019–21).
Bihar has a total fertility rate of about 3.0 (NFHS-5, 2019–21).
Fertility is linked to, for example, female literacy, women's status, income and health care.

notes.b: India was early to try to control population growth, but one campaign went badly wrong.
points: India launched the world's first national family-planning programme in 1952, to slow population growth.
Forced sterilisation campaigns during the Emergency (1975–77), under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, caused a backlash.
Today the focus is on education, health and voluntary family planning.

notes.b: The sex ratio is the number of females per 1,000 males. India has fewer females than males, and fewer girls still among children.
points: Census 2011 recorded 943 females per 1,000 males.
The child sex ratio (age 0–6) was 918 in Census 2011.
Son preference (valuing sons above daughters) and sex-selective abortion cause the imbalance.
Prenatal sex determination (finding out the sex of an unborn child) was banned by law in 1994, so that it could not be used for selection.
The 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' campaign, launched in 2015, means 'Save the daughter, educate the daughter'.

notes.b: Population structure means the share of people at each age. India's is young.
points: India has a young population, shown by a broad-based pyramid (a population pyramid with many children at the bottom).
The demographic dividend is the economic gain if young workers find jobs.
A large young population puts pressure on schools and jobs, because many people need places and work.

notes.b: Literacy, the share of people who can read and write, differs by sex and by state.
points: Census 2011 literacy was about 74% overall: about 82% for men and about 65% for women.
Kerala had the highest literacy, about 94%; Bihar had the lowest, about 62%.

notes.b: Population distribution is explained by physical and human factors. Dense areas combine good land, water and economic opportunity.
points: The Ganges plain is dense, due to fertile alluvium, water, flat land and a long history of settlement.
The deltas and coastal plains, such as Kerala and West Bengal, are dense.
Around the large cities, such as Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata, population is dense.
Human factors: history, farming, industry, transport and government policy.
notes.tip: Population distribution is set as a Higher Level question: account for dense and sparse areas, explaining each with both physical and human factors.

notes.b: Sparse areas are where the climate, relief, soils or water make living difficult.
points: The Thar Desert is sparse because of aridity (extreme dryness).
The Himalayas are sparse because of cold temperatures, steep slopes and thin soils.
The forested hills of the north-east are sparse.
The central plateaus are sparse.
Physical factors: climate, relief, soils and water.

notes.b: Density is the number of people per square kilometre. Use these Census 2011 figures to support your answers.
points: Census 2011 national density was 382 people per km².
Bihar is the densest state, at about 1,100 people per km².
Arunachal Pradesh is the least dense state, at about 17 people per km².
Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state, with about 200 million people (Census 2011).

notes.b: Migration is the movement of people from one place to live in another. In India it flows from poor regions to richer ones and abroad.
points: Internal rural-to-urban migration moves people from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh to Mumbai, Delhi and other cities, because cities offer more work.
During the COVID-19 lockdown from March 2020, millions of migrant workers walked or travelled home from the cities.
Emigration (leaving India to live abroad) to the Gulf, especially from Kerala, and to Western countries is significant.
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances (money sent home by migrants working abroad) (2020s).

notes.b: India has a huge number of languages, which makes language an important human process.
points: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution recognises 22 languages.
Census 2011 found 121 languages, each spoken by 10,000 or more people.

notes.b: A language family is a group of related languages. India's languages fall mainly into two families, split between north and south.
points: Indo-Aryan languages are spoken in the north, for example Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati and Punjabi.
Dravidian languages are spoken in the south, for example Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam.

notes.b: Hindi is the most widely spoken language, but its status is often misunderstood.
points: Hindi is the most widely spoken language: about 44% of Indians reported it as their mother tongue in Census 2011; Bengali is second, at about 8%.
The Hindi belt covers Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi.
Hindi, in Devanagari script, is the official language of the Union (the central government); the Constitution names no national language.
The Official Languages Act of 1963 kept English in official use.
notes.tip: Hindi is the official language of the Union, not a 'national language'. The Constitution names no national language.

notes.b: Language became the basis on which India's states were drawn.
points: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew state boundaries along language lines, so most states are language regions, which keeps each language community together.
Andhra State, created in 1953, was the first state formed for a language (Telugu).

notes.b: Language has caused political conflict, especially over the place of Hindi.
points: Resistance to Hindi being imposed, especially in Tamil Nadu, led to the anti-Hindi agitation of 1965.
Schools use a three-language formula, a compromise that teaches several languages, such as Hindi and English.

notes.b: English plays a special role because it belongs to no single Indian region.
points: English is a colonial legacy (left over from British rule) and a link language between states, because speakers of different Indian languages can use it to communicate.
It is an economic advantage for IT, outsourcing and global business, as it was a reason for IT growth.

notes.b: India has a Hindu majority but also very large minorities. These Census 2011 figures show the mix.
points: Census 2011: Hindus about 80% of the population.
Muslims about 14%, about 172 million people, a very large minority.
Christians about 2.3%, Sikhs about 1.7%, Buddhists about 0.7% and Jains about 0.4%.

notes.b: Some religions are concentrated in particular states, while others are spread widely.
points: Sikhs are concentrated in Punjab, the only Sikh-majority state, where their holiest shrine stands.
Christians form the majority in Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya.
Muslims are spread throughout India, and form the majority in Jammu and Kashmir.
Hindus are found everywhere.

notes.h: India as a birthplace of religions
notes.b: Four world religions began in India, and their holy places draw pilgrims.
points: India is the birthplace of four religions, so it has many holy places: Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism.
Varanasi is a Hindu holy city, so it draws pilgrims.
Bodh Gaya, Bihar, is where the Buddha attained enlightenment.
The Golden Temple at Amritsar, Punjab, is the holiest Sikh shrine.
notes.tip: Culture questions ask about the importance of religion, language and other cultural factors, so India's religion and language material serves.

notes.b: Religion shaped India's modern borders when British rule ended.
points: In August 1947 British India was divided into India and the Muslim-majority Pakistan.
More than 10 million people were displaced (forced to leave their homes) and hundreds of thousands were killed, because of mass migration and communal violence.
East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971, which is why Bangladesh now lies on India's eastern side.

notes.b: India's constitution treats all religions equally, but tension between religious communities has continued.
points: India is constitutionally a secular state (the state favours no religion).
Communal tension has persisted: the demolition of the Babri Masjid mosque at Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, in 1992 was followed by riots.
Kashmir: Article 370, which gave Jammu and Kashmir special status, was revoked in August 2019.

notes.b: Caste divides Indian society into hereditary groups and is closely tied to Hinduism, though it is not a religion.
points: Caste is a hereditary social system linked to Hinduism; it is a social system, not a religion.
Dalits were formerly called 'untouchables'.
The Constitution, in force from 26 January 1950, abolished untouchability.
Reserved places (quotas) in education, government jobs and parliament are given to Scheduled Castes (about 17% of the population) and Scheduled Tribes (about 9%), Census 2011.
Caste still affects rural life, marriage and politics, even though untouchability is illegal.
notes.tip: Caste is a social system, not a religion. Don't say caste was abolished: untouchability was.

notes.b: Religious beliefs and festivals shape what people produce, eat and spend.
points: Sacred cattle support dairying, because Hindus keep them for milk.
Vegetarian diets increase demand for pulses and milk, since they replace meat.
Pilgrimage tourism draws visitors to Varanasi and the Kumbh Mela.
Festivals such as Diwali boost consumer spending, because people buy gifts and goods.

notes.b: Urbanisation is the growing share of people who live in towns and cities. India is still mostly rural but is urbanising fast, because people move to cities for work.
points: Census 2011: about 31% of India's population was urban, up from about 17% in 1951.
There were 53 urban agglomerations (a city together with its built-up suburbs) with over 1 million people.
India is still mostly rural but is urbanising fast.

notes.b: India's three largest urban agglomerations are Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.
points: Greater Mumbai had about 18.4 million people in Census 2011.
Delhi had about 16.3 million people in Census 2011.
Kolkata had about 14.1 million people in Census 2011.

notes.b: Mumbai is the expected case study for an urban area. Other cities are described separately, so you can choose one to learn in full.
points: Site: originally seven islands on the west coast, joined by land reclamation, with a deep, sheltered natural harbour.
The British East India Company developed it as a port, using its harbour; the Gateway of India marks it.
Cotton mills grew in the 19th century, so industry added to the port's trade, drawing on the cotton of Gujarat and Maharashtra.
Mumbai is India's financial capital: the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India, and the Bombay Stock Exchange, founded in 1875, Asia's oldest.
Bollywood, the Hindi film industry, is based in Mumbai.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Navi Mumbai is one of India's main container ports.
The city was renamed Mumbai from Bombay in 1995.
Mumbai is not the political capital; New Delhi is.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the factors that influenced the development of one urban area, or the reasons for its growth. Mumbai is the expected case study.

notes.b: Rapid growth has left Mumbai with severe problems, and planners have tried several responses.
points: Dharavi, in central Mumbai, is one of Asia's largest slums, a result of rapid growth and high housing costs.
Overcrowding, high housing costs, congestion and overcrowded suburban trains are problems.
The flood of 26 July 2005 saw about 944 mm of rain fall at Santacruz in one day, paralysing the city.
Water supply and sanitation (sewage and clean water systems) are inadequate, because services have not kept pace with growth.
Navi Mumbai, begun in the 1970s, is a planned twin city across the harbour, built to relieve pressure on Mumbai.
Responses include slum redevelopment and new metro lines.

notes.b: Kolkata is a shorter alternative case study, a colonial port city that lost ground after independence.
points: Kolkata was founded in 1690 by the British East India Company (Job Charnock).
It was the capital of British India until 1911, so it grew as an imperial centre.
It is a port on the Hooghly with jute mills and engineering industries.
Partition in 1947 cut Kolkata off from the jute-growing lands that became East Pakistan, which hurt its jute industry.
India's first metro opened in Kolkata in 1984.
Kolkata has congestion and slums.
notes.tip: Kolkata was the British capital until 1911; Delhi and New Delhi have been the capital since. Mumbai is the financial capital, not the political one.

notes.b: Bengaluru is another shorter case study, a city whose growth rests on IT.
points: Bengaluru is India's IT capital, growing on the base of the IT industry (firms such as Infosys and Wipro are based there).
It is called the 'Garden City'.
It sits on the Deccan Plateau at about 900 m, so altitude gives a mild climate.
Problems of rapid growth include traffic congestion, water shortages, and the loss of lakes and green space.

notes.b: Delhi is India's capital city, with a planned imperial district beside the older city.
points: Delhi has been the national capital since 1911, so it grew as a seat of government, when it became capital of British India.
New Delhi was designed by Edwin Lutyens and inaugurated in 1931.
The National Capital Region includes Gurugram (Haryana) and Noida (Uttar Pradesh).
Severe winter air pollution affects the city, which is worsened by stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana.

notes.b: The government has tried to plan new cities and improve existing ones.
points: Chandigarh was planned (laid out in advance) by Le Corbusier in the 1950s and is the capital of Punjab and Haryana.
The Smart Cities Mission, launched in 2015, covers 100 cities.
Metro systems are part of urban policy.

notes.b: Fast growth has outrun services in Indian cities, which causes these shared problems.
points: Census 2011: about 65 million people lived in slums (crowded areas of poor housing).
Informal employment is widespread, so many workers have no secure income.
Water supply, sanitation and waste disposal are inadequate.
Air pollution and traffic congestion are serious problems, because of crowding and vehicles.

notes.b: Most Indians still live in the countryside, in a very large number of villages.
points: Census 2011: about 833 million people (about 69%) lived in rural areas.
There are about 640,000 villages.

notes.b: Rural areas share a set of linked problems that keep incomes low.
points: Poverty, small holdings and landlessness, and debt.
Dependence on the monsoon, so a poor year hits incomes, and under-employment (not enough work through the year).
Poor services, such as water, sanitation, health and schools.
Lower literacy, especially among women.
Caste discrimination.
Out-migration of young men, who leave to find work, leaving villages short of workers.

notes.b: The government has launched many programmes to improve rural life.
points: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) created Panchayati Raj, elected village councils, with one-third of seats reserved for women.
MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of paid work a year to each rural household, to give a basic income and reduce under-employment.
The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (2000) is a rural roads programme.
The Swachh Bharat Mission, launched on 2 October 2014, builds toilets, to improve sanitation.
The government declared every village electrified in April 2018.
PM-KISAN income support, which pays ₹6,000 a year to landholding farm families.
Self-help groups and microcredit (small loans) for women, so they can start small businesses.

notes.h: Kerala and Bihar: contrasting rural outcomes
notes.b: Two states show how human and economic processes interact to give very different results.
points: Kerala: high literacy (about 94%), so lower fertility, good health, and remittances from migrants in the Gulf.
Bihar: low literacy (about 62%), high fertility, and out-migration.
The contrast shows human processes and economic processes interacting.

notes.b: Development is uneven across India, so some regions are far richer than others.
points: The more developed west and south include Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.
The poorer north and east, such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
The 'BIMARU' states are Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh; the term was coined in the 1980s and resembles the Hindi word for sick.
This is a core–periphery pattern within the subcontinent: a wealthier core region and a poorer outer region.

notes.b: The syllabus asks how economic, human and physical processes interact. These chains link the topics above and can be used in conclusions.
points: Monsoon, then farming calendar, then rural incomes, then migration, then urban slums.
Chota Nagpur minerals, then steel, because the coal and iron ore are on site, then an industrial region.
English as a colonial legacy, then IT services, then Bengaluru's growth.
Religion, then dairying and pilgrimage tourism.
notes.tip: Human processes questions ask for the impact of two of population dynamics, language, religion, urban development and rural development on the region's development.
