factCards.term: Sketch map of India: recommended features and how to place them
factCards.definition: Relief: outline the Himalayas as a band along the northern border, or the Deccan south of the Narmada. River: the Ganges from Uttarakhand south-east past Varanasi to its delta. Cities as dots: Mumbai (west coast), Kolkata (on the Hooghly). Farming region: outline Punjab.

factCards.term: South-west monsoon: how it forms, in sequence
factCards.definition: Heating of the land in early summer creates low pressure over north-west India and Tibet; the ITCZ moves north; south-east trades cross the equator and turn (Coriolis force) into moist south-west winds; the jet stream shifts north of the Himalayas and the monsoon bursts.

factCards.term: India's three seasons and the timing of the monsoon
factCards.definition: Hot season, March–May; wet south-west monsoon, June–September, reaching Kerala about 1 June and all India by mid-July and bringing about three-quarters of the year's rain; cool dry season, October–February, when north-east winds blow off the land.

factCards.term: Monsoon branches: where the heaviest rain falls and why
factCards.definition: The Arabian Sea branch rises over the Western Ghats, soaking the Konkan and Malabar coasts; the Deccan lies in rain shadow. The Bay of Bengal branch hits the north-east hills (Mawsynram, Cherrapunji), then turns west along the Ganges plain, drier westwards.

factCards.term: Monsoon hazards, and why the monsoon matters to India
factCards.definition: A late or weak monsoon brings drought, a heavy one floods; cyclones strike the east coast (Odisha super cyclone, October 1999, about 10,000 deaths); climate change makes it more erratic. It sets the farming calendar, refills reservoirs and groundwater, and affects GDP.

factCards.term: India's main soil types: where they are found and what they grow
factCards.definition: Alluvial: Indo-Gangetic Plain, most extensive and fertile. Black (regur): Deccan Traps, cotton. Red: south and east Deccan, millets, groundnuts, pulses. Laterite: Western Ghats and Kerala, tea, coffee, cashew with fertiliser. Desert: Thar, productive only where irrigated.

factCards.term: The Himalayas: formation, highest peak and effects on India
factCards.definition: Young fold mountains formed as the Indian plate collides with the Eurasian plate (from about 50 million years ago); Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) is India's highest peak. Effects: block cold Central Asian air; trigger monsoon rain; feed snow-fed rivers; earthquakes; sparse settlement.

factCards.term: The Deccan Plateau and the Ghats: key features
factCards.definition: An ancient, stable shield of crystalline rock, once part of Gondwanaland, tilting west to east so most rivers flow east; minerals on the Chota Nagpur Plateau; Deccan Traps basalt in the north-west; the steep Western Ghats (UNESCO 2012) and lower, broken Eastern Ghats.

factCards.term: The Ganges: source, course, cities and delta
factCards.definition: Rises as the Bhagirathi at Gaumukh (Gangotri Glacier, Uttarakhand) and becomes the Ganga at Devprayag; flows about 2,500 km past Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj (where the Yamuna joins), Varanasi and Patna to the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, the world's largest.

factCards.term: Indian agriculture: importance and human problems
factCards.definition: About 55% of workers farmed (Census 2011), yet farming gives under a fifth of GDP: low productivity. Holdings average about 1.1 hectares, 86% under 2 hectares (2015–16), subdivided at inheritance; landless labourers; little credit, so debt; middlemen; post-harvest losses.

factCards.term: Types of agriculture in India and where they are found
factCards.definition: Subsistence farming on small plots; wet-rice (paddy) in the wet east, south and deltas; irrigated commercial wheat in Punjab and Haryana; tea plantations in Assam, Darjeeling and the Nilgiri Hills; coffee in Karnataka; cotton on black soils; jute in West Bengal; dairying.

factCards.term: Physical advantages and problems for farming in India
factCards.definition: Advantages: heat allows two or three crops a year; monsoon rain; fertile alluvium and black soil; flat plains; perennial Himalayan rivers for irrigation. Problems: unreliable monsoon; poor laterite and desert soils; steep slopes; erosion; salinisation; falling water tables.

factCards.term: Green Revolution: methods, results and costs
factCards.definition: From the mid-1960s: high-yielding wheat (Borlaug; brought in by M. S. Swaminathan) and rice, fertilisers and irrigation. Grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million (2022–23). Gains went mainly to Punjab and Haryana; costs: groundwater loss, debt.

factCards.term: White Revolution: how India became the largest milk producer
factCards.definition: Operation Flood (1970), run by the National Dairy Development Board under Verghese Kurien, spread co-operative dairying on the Amul model (Anand, Gujarat). Religion helps: the cow is sacred to Hindus, so cattle are kept for milk and draught, not beef.

factCards.term: Indian farming: government support and recent conflict
factCards.definition: Minimum support prices, with grain bought by the Food Corporation of India; PM-KISAN (2019) pays ₹6,000 a year to landholding farm families. Conflict: the 2020–21 farmers' protests against three farm laws, repealed in November 2021; stubble burning worsening Delhi's smog.

factCards.term: India's mining and energy: named examples
factCards.definition: The Chota Nagpur Plateau (Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh) holds most coal and iron ore. India is the second-largest coal producer; coal gives about 70% of electricity. Mumbai High oilfield (1974). Bhadla Solar Park; target of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

factCards.term: Raw materials and the location of Indian industry: three examples
factCards.definition: Tata Iron and Steel (1907) at Jamshedpur used Chota Nagpur coal and iron ore; cotton from black soils fed mills in Mumbai and Ahmedabad, the 'Manchester of India'; jute from the Ganges delta fed mills along the Hooghly near Kolkata.

factCards.term: Government policy and Indian manufacturing, 1951 to today
factCards.definition: 1951–1991: five-year plans, state steel plants (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur), protection, the Licence Raj. 1991: Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh scrapped most licences, cut tariffs and opened to foreign investment. Later: SEZ Act 2005, Make in India 2014, incentives from 2020.

factCards.term: Labour, markets and infrastructure as factors for Indian industry
factCards.definition: Labour: a huge, young, low-cost workforce and engineers from the IITs (first at Kharagpur, 1951). Markets: over 1.4 billion people and a growing middle class. Infrastructure: ports, railways, the Golden Quadrilateral, but power cuts and congestion raise costs.

factCards.term: India's main manufacturing regions
factCards.definition: Mumbai–Pune; Ahmedabad–Vadodara (Gujarat); the Hooghly belt round Kolkata; Chota Nagpur and the Damodar valley (Jamshedpur); the Delhi National Capital Region (Gurugram, Noida); Bengaluru, Chennai, Coimbatore. Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha have less industry.

factCards.term: Key Indian industries with named examples
factCards.definition: Steel: second-largest producer. Cars: Maruti Suzuki (1983) at Gurugram and Manesar; Hyundai at Chennai. Medicines: Hyderabad; the Serum Institute, Pune, the largest vaccine maker. Electronics: Foxconn iPhones at Sriperumbudur. Aerospace: HAL and ISRO in Bengaluru.

factCards.term: Challenges facing manufacturing in India
factCards.definition: Poor infrastructure and power; land conflicts (at Singur in 2008 protests forced Tata to move its Nano plant to Sanand, Gujarat); bureaucracy; competition from China; accidents (Bhopal gas leak, 1984); old industries declining, as Mumbai's mills closed after the 1982 strike.

factCards.term: India's IT industry: centres and reasons for growth
factCards.definition: Centres: Bengaluru ('Silicon Valley of India'), Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Gurugram, Noida. Reasons: many English-speaking graduates; the IITs; low wages; a time difference allowing round-the-clock work for the USA; 1991 liberalisation and software technology parks.

factCards.term: Tourism in India: name eight attractions
factCards.definition: The Taj Mahal, Agra, built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal (UNESCO 1983); the Golden Triangle of Delhi, Agra and Jaipur; Goa's beaches; Kerala's backwaters at Alappuzha; Varanasi's ghats; Jim Corbett National Park (1936) and Kaziranga; the Golden Temple, Amritsar.

factCards.term: Tourism in India: why tourists come, and government support
factCards.definition: Mughal and Hindu monuments and festivals; varied landscapes; a warm, dry winter (October–March) matching Europe's; low costs; yoga, Ayurveda and medical tourism. Support: 'Incredible India' (2002); e-visas (2014); low-cost airlines. About 11 million foreign arrivals in 2019.

factCards.term: Tourism in India: positive and negative impacts
factCards.definition: Positive: jobs in hotels, guiding, crafts and transport; foreign currency; infrastructure; protection of heritage and wildlife. Negative: crowding and pollution (air pollution yellows the Taj Mahal's marble); water shortages and waste in Goa; cultural erosion; seasonality.

factCards.term: Transport in India: two named types with facts
factCards.definition: Rail: first train Bombay–Thane, 16 April 1853; Indian Railways runs about 68,000 km and employs over 1 million; Vande Bharat trains (2019); Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed line being built. Road: the Golden Quadrilateral (from 2001) links Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

factCards.term: India's population: size, growth and demographic transition
factCards.definition: Census 1951 about 361 million; Census 2011 about 1.21 billion; India passed China in 2023 (UN). Death rates fell first (medicine, vaccination, Green Revolution food) while births stayed high; fertility was 2.0 in 2019–21 (NFHS-5), below replacement: late stage 3.

factCards.term: India's population policy and sex ratio
factCards.definition: First national family-planning programme in the world (1952); forced sterilisation in the Emergency (1975–77) caused a backlash. Census 2011: 943 females per 1,000 males (918 aged 0–6), due to son preference; sex determination banned 1994; 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' (2015).

factCards.term: Population distribution in India: dense and sparse areas, with reasons
factCards.definition: Dense: the Ganges plain (fertile alluvium, water, flat land), deltas, the Kerala and West Bengal coasts, big cities. Sparse: the Thar (aridity), the Himalayas (cold, steep, thin soils), north-east hills. Census 2011: Bihar about 1,100 per km², Arunachal Pradesh about 17.

factCards.term: Languages in India: diversity, families and official status
factCards.definition: 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule; 121 spoken by 10,000 or more (Census 2011). Indo-Aryan in the north (Hindi, Bengali), Dravidian in the south (Tamil, Telugu). Hindi, mother tongue of about 44%, is the Union's official language; states were redrawn by language in 1956.

factCards.term: Religion in India: composition and distribution
factCards.definition: Census 2011: Hindu about 80%; Muslim about 14% (about 172 million); Christian 2.3%; Sikh 1.7%; Buddhist 0.7%; Jain 0.4%. Sikhs are concentrated in Punjab; Christians are the majority in Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya; Muslims in Jammu and Kashmir.

factCards.term: The caste system in India today
factCards.definition: A hereditary social system linked to Hinduism, not a religion. The Constitution (1950) abolished untouchability; Scheduled Castes (about 17%) and Scheduled Tribes (about 9%) have reserved places in education, government jobs and parliament. Caste still shapes rural life.

factCards.term: Mumbai: factors in its growth
factCards.definition: Seven islands joined by reclamation round a deep, sheltered harbour; a port built up by the East India Company; 19th-century cotton mills; the financial capital (Reserve Bank, Bombay Stock Exchange 1875); Bollywood; rural migrants. Greater Mumbai: about 18.4 million (2011).

factCards.term: Mumbai: urban problems and responses
factCards.definition: Dharavi, one of Asia's largest slums; overcrowding, high housing costs, packed suburban trains; the 26 July 2005 flood (about 944 mm in a day at Santacruz); poor water and sanitation. Responses: Navi Mumbai twin city (from the 1970s), slum redevelopment, metro lines.

factCards.term: Rural India: problems and development policies
factCards.definition: About 833 million rural people (69%, 2011) face poverty, debt, tiny holdings and poor services. Policies: Panchayati Raj (1992, a third of seats for women); MGNREGA (2005, 100 days' paid work); rural roads (2000); Swachh Bharat (2014); village electrification (2018).

questions.prompt: Examine how two factors have influenced the development of secondary economic activity in India.
questions.model: Raw materials: the Chota Nagpur Plateau holds much of India's coal and iron ore, the basis of the steel industry. The Tata Iron and Steel Company, founded in 1907 at Jamshedpur, was India's first large steel works, sited on Chota Nagpur coal and iron ore. The state steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur were built with Soviet, West German and British help. Cotton grown on black soils supported textile mills in Mumbai and Ahmedabad. Jute grown in the Ganges delta supported jute mills along the Hooghly near Kolkata. Government policy: from 1951 five-year plans promoted state-led industrialisation behind protection from imports. The Licence Raj required permits to start or expand a factory, which made industry inefficient. The 1991 reforms under P. V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment, after which manufacturing grew rapidly. Make in India (2014), Special Economic Zones (Act of 2005) and production-linked incentives from 2020 have since aimed to attract firms to chosen sites.

questions.prompt: Account for the distribution of population in India.
questions.model: India had a density of 382 people per km² in Census 2011, but population is very unevenly spread. Dense areas: the Ganges plain has fertile alluvium, water, flat land and a long history of settlement, and Bihar is the densest state at about 1,100 per km². The deltas and coastal plains, such as Kerala and West Bengal, are dense because of fertile land, water and access to the sea and trade. Cities such as Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata draw dense populations because of industry, jobs and transport. Sparse areas: the Thar Desert is sparse because of aridity and low rainfall. The Himalayas are sparse because of cold temperatures, steep slopes and thin soils. The forested hills of the north-east and the central plateaus are sparse because of relief, soils and limited farming. Human factors such as history, farming, industry, transport and government policy reinforce these physical patterns. The contrast is clearest between Bihar, at about 1,100 per km², and Arunachal Pradesh, at about 17 per km².
